chapters.title: Chapter 1: Supervised Learning and Classification Fundamentals
chapters.description: Introduces the core concepts of supervised learning with a focus on classification tasks. Covers the mathematical formulation of learning from labeled examples, common loss functions, and evaluation metrics used to assess classifier performance.
subtopics: Problem setup: training, validation, test sets
Classification vs. regression
Loss functions: cross-entropy, log loss, hinge loss
Output representations: logits, probabilities, softmax
Training basics: gradient descent, mini-batch updates
Evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision/recall, ROC curve and AUROC, F1-score
Model selection and overfitting/underfitting

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Tabular Data — Structure, Types, and Preprocessing
chapters.description: Explains the nature of tabular datasets and standard preprocessing steps required before applying learning algorithms. Emphasizes heterogeneous feature types and practical techniques to prepare tabular inputs.
subtopics: Feature types: numerical (continuous), ordinal, categorical, binary, timestamps, text
Missing data handling: imputation strategies
Scaling and normalization: standardization, min–max, robust scalers
Encoding categorical variables: one-hot, ordinal, target encoding
Binning and discretization
Feature typing and metadata (feature names and descriptions)
Serialization of tabular rows to text (basic approaches and use cases)

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Feature Engineering for Tabular Learning
chapters.description: Covers manual and automated feature construction techniques commonly used in tabular modeling, including creation of rule-based features, interaction terms, and feature selection strategies.
subtopics: Motivation for feature engineering
Basic transforms: polynomial features, interactions, log transforms
Binning and categorical grouping
Rule-based feature creation (if–then conditions, thresholds)
Automatic feature construction: feature crosses, feature hashing
Feature selection and importance: filter, wrapper, embedded methods
Assessing feature usefulness: univariate metrics, mutual information, AUROC per feature

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Linear Models and Probabilistic Outputs
chapters.description: Details linear predictive models commonly applied to tabular tasks, how they produce probabilities, and techniques for training and regularization in low-data regimes.
subtopics: Linear models: linear regression, logistic regression
Interpreting weights and decision boundaries
From logits to probabilities: sigmoid and softmax
Optimization algorithms: SGD, Adam, learning rate schedules
Regularization: L1, L2, and constraints (e.g., non-negativity)
Bias terms and calibration
Simple thresholding and scoring rules

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Ensemble Methods and Bagging
chapters.description: Presents ensemble learning concepts that combine multiple models or feature sets to improve robustness and accuracy, with attention to bagging and variance reduction.
subtopics: Motivation and types of ensembles: bagging, boosting, stacking
Bootstrap aggregation (bagging): sampling instances and/or features
Random forests as an instance of bagging + feature randomness
Averaging probabilities vs. voting
Diversity, bias–variance trade-off, and ensemble size considerations
Self-consistency and majority consensus ideas
Practical ensemble design and computational costs

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Few-Shot and Low-Resource Learning
chapters.description: Surveys methods for learning with very limited labeled data, including transfer learning, meta-learning, and strategies that leverage other information sources to improve sample efficiency.
subtopics: Definition of few-shot learning and k‑shot evaluation protocols
Transfer learning and pretraining for tabular data
Meta-learning paradigms (model-agnostic, metric-based approaches)
Semi-supervised and self-supervised methods for tabular data
Synthetic data generation and pretraining with simulated distributions
Data augmentation challenges for tabular data
Evaluation practices and baselines for few-shot settings

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Transformer-Based Large Language Models (LLMs)
chapters.description: Provides an overview of transformer architectures and large language models: their training, capabilities, limitations, and practical considerations when accessed via API.
subtopics: Transformer architecture: attention, positional encodings, layers
Pretraining objectives and data sources
Capabilities arising from scale and pretraining
Context window (prompt length) and its implications
Temperature, top-p (nucleus) sampling, and decoding parameters
API access models vs. fine-tuning access
Limitations: hallucinations, memorization, and distributional biases

chapters.title: Chapter 8: In-Context Learning and Prompt Engineering
chapters.description: Explores how LLMs can perform tasks through carefully designed prompts and few-shot examples without parameter updates, discussing strategies to elicit better reasoning and outputs.
subtopics: In-context learning concept and examples
Designing prompts: task description, examples, format instructions
Few-shot example selection and ordering effects
Chain-of-thought and structured prompting for improved reasoning
Controlling LLM stochasticity: temperature and sampling strategies
Prompt length trade-offs and context management
Failure modes and mitigation techniques

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Methods
chapters.description: Introduces techniques that adapt large pretrained models with few trainable parameters, enabling improved task performance without full-model training.
subtopics: Motivation for parameter-efficient tuning
Adapters, prefix tuning, and prompt tuning
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and IA3 basics
When to fine-tune vs. when to use in-context learning
Computation and memory considerations
Evaluation differences between tuning and inference-only approaches

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Using LLMs for Tabular Problems — Textual Interfaces and Prior Work
chapters.description: Summarizes approaches that interface LLMs with tabular data by converting tables to text, extracting knowledge, and performing predictions or guidance.
subtopics: Serialization strategies for rows and columns into natural language
Leveraging feature names and descriptions as prompts
Examples of LLM-based tabular methods (in-context, tuning-based)
Practical limitations: per-sample inference cost and prompt size
Combining LLM outputs with classical ML models
Case studies and observed benefits in low-shot regimes

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Rule-Based Models, Decision Trees, and Interpretability
chapters.description: Covers models and representations that produce human-interpretable rules, how rules can be used as features, and techniques to extract, evaluate, and parse rules.
subtopics: Decision trees and rule extraction from trees
Rule-based classifiers and association rules
Structure of a rule: antecedent, consequent, logical operators
Converting rules into binary indicator features
Evaluating rule quality: support, confidence, and discriminative power
Trade-offs between interpretability and predictive power
Use of rules for debugging and domain validation

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Programmatic Parsing and LLM Code Generation
chapters.description: Describes how language models can generate code from natural language, techniques for parsing noisy outputs, and safe execution considerations when converting text to executable feature-generation code.
subtopics: Code generation capabilities of LLMs (natural language to Python)
Parsing natural language rules into structured forms
Handling syntactic variation and noisy outputs
Validation and unit testing of generated code
Security and sandboxing when executing generated code (exec risks)
Strategies for robust parsing: templates, strict formats, and confirmation prompts
Fallback and error-handling mechanisms

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Experimental Design, Evaluation, and Ablation Studies
chapters.description: Covers best practices for designing experiments in machine learning research, including cross-validation, hyperparameter selection, ablations, and reporting of results.
subtopics: Train/validation/test splits and k-fold cross-validation
Hyperparameter tuning protocols and preventing leakage
Ablation studies to isolate component contributions
Reporting averages, variances, and statistical significance
Measuring runtime, cost, and inference latency
Reproducibility practices and code/data reporting
Choosing meaningful baselines

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Spurious Correlations, Robustness, and Bias in Models
chapters.description: Examines the phenomenon of spurious correlations in low-data settings, the role of prior knowledge and bias introduced by pretraining, and strategies to detect and mitigate fragile predictors.
subtopics: Definition and examples of spurious correlations
Effects of small sample sizes on learning spurious patterns
Role of prior knowledge and model priors in shaping predictions
Bias and fairness issues arising from pretraining corpora
Robustness testing: adding irrelevant features and stress tests
Mitigation strategies: regularization, feature validation, causal reasoning
Interpreting model decisions to detect harmful biases

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Practical Deployment Considerations for LLM-Augmented Systems
chapters.description: Discusses real-world aspects of deploying systems that combine LLMs and classical ML for tabular tasks: API constraints, cost/latency trade-offs, batching strategies, and privacy/ethical considerations.
subtopics: API access limits, rate limiting, and prompt size constraints
Latency and cost analysis of per-sample LLM inference vs. offline processing
Batching, caching, and parallelization tactics
Privacy and data leakage risks when sending data to external APIs
Monitoring, logging, and model drift detection
Governance: bias audits, human-in-the-loop checks, and compliance
Scaling strategies and when to consider on-premise or fine-tuning alternatives
